chunks.text: On November 21 1915 a ship called Endurance sank in the Weddell Sea near Antarctica All twenty-eight men of her expedition were still alive But they had no ship no radio and no way to tell the outside world where they were They were stranded on drifting sea ice

with three small lifeboats and whatever supplies they had managed to save To get everyone home six men would eventually have to cross more than eight hundred miles of open ocean in a boat barely seven metres long The other twenty-two would have to wait without knowing whether those six had survived

And even if the boat reached help someone would still have to find a way back through the ice In 1914 Ernest Shackleton set out to lead the first expedition across Antarctica travelling from one coast to the other by way of the South Pole His ship Endurance was supposed to carry the expedition

into the Weddell Sea where the crossing would begin But in January 1915 moving pack ice closed around the vessel For months Captain Frank Worsley tracked their position while the crew maintained the ship and waited for a chance to escape The sea ice moved with the winds and currents Instead of carrying

them toward their destination it took the trapped ship wherever it drifted Then in October the pressure became too great The wooden hull began to give way Water entered and on October 27 Shackleton ordered the men to abandon ship They carried three lifeboats provisions and equipment

onto the surrounding ice On November 21 Endurance sank The expedition had never reached its starting point on the Antarctic continent Now the men had to find another way home Shackleton first tried moving toward land on foot But hauling heavy lifeboats across

broken ice proved almost impossible Ridges blocked their path cracks forced detours and the men made little progress They abandoned the march and established a camp on a drifting floe For months they waited as the current carried them north They rationed their food hunted seals and penguins

and kept the lifeboats ready In April 1916 the ice beneath them began breaking apart On April 9 they launched their boats into the water For nearly a week the crews rowed and sailed between moving floes struggling to reach Elephant Island On April 15 all twenty-eight

men finally landed They had reached solid ground but Elephant Island was uninhabited and far from normal shipping routes No rescue ship knew they were there Shackleton decided that a small crew must leave to find help Their destination was South Georgia roughly 1 300 kilometres

over 800 miles to the northeast across the Scotia Sea There were whaling stations on the island If the men could reach one they could obtain help and organise a rescue Their only suitable vessel was the largest lifeboat the James Caird The carpenter Harry McNish raised its sides fitted

a partial covering of wood and canvas and worked to make the hull more watertight Shackleton initially intended to leave Thomas Crean on Elephant Island to assist his second-in-command Frank Wild But after discussing the plan he decided to take Crean on the ocean crossing instead On April 24 Shackleton departed

with Worsley McNish Crean Timothy McCarthy and John Vincent Twenty-two men remained under Wild's command Wild's first challenge was finding shelter An ice cave offered protection from the wind but it was wet and unsuitable for living in The men abandoned it Instead they

built low stone walls and used two overturned lifeboats canvas and other salvaged materials to form a roof The shelter was cramped but it gave the men somewhere to live as winter approached While Wild organised life inside it the James Caird was already far out at sea Finding South Georgia

required more than sailing northeast It was a small island in an enormous ocean If the James Caird passed too far to either side the men might miss it entirely Worsley had to navigate with a sextant a compass and calculations of their estimated progress He needed the sun to determine their position

But cloud cover heavy seas and the constant movement of the boat made observations difficult During the crossing he obtained only four usable observations of the sun Between them he estimated their position from the course steered and distance travelled adjusting whenever new evidence allowed The others kept the boat moving

and afloat They worked in watches handling the sails steering and bailing water Ice accumulated on the vessel adding weight that had to be removed After nearly two weeks at sea they were approaching where Worsley calculated South Georgia should be On May 8 land appeared through a break in the clouds

They had found the island But heavy seas and dangerous surf prevented an immediate landing For two more days they remained offshore searching for a safe approach On May 10 the six men finally landed in King Haakon Bay on South Georgia's western coast The whaling stations were on the other side of

the island With the James Caird and its crew in their exhausted condition attempting to reach those stations by sailing around the coast was too dangerous Shackleton decided to cross the mountains instead McNish Vincent and McCarthy remained behind Shackleton Worsley and Crean set out on foot on May

19 There was no established route through the mountains and glaciers At one steep icy descent Worsley and Crean held the rope while Shackleton used a carpenter's adze to cut steps into the ice Descending roughly five hundred feet took them about two hours Then the three continued across snowfields and ridges

searching for a passage toward the inhabited coast On May 20 after approximately thirty-six hours of travelling they reached the whaling station at Stromness The three men left on South Georgia's western shore were subsequently brought to safety But no news of any of this had reached Elephant Island

Wild and the other twenty-one men were still waiting Inside their shelter they maintained a daily routine gathered food when they could and endured the Antarctic winter without knowing whether the James Caird had reached its destination Wild kept the group organised Each day he rolled up his own sleeping bag repeating

that Shackleton might arrive that day The others continued the work of maintaining the camp and finding food Days passed Then weeks Shackleton's first rescue attempt aboard the whaling ship Southern Sky was stopped by pack ice The next attempt using the Uruguayan vessel Instituto de Pesca No 1

and a later voyage aboard the schooner Emma also failed to reach Elephant Island Three attempts had failed and the men on the island still had no news As winter continued food became increasingly scarce By late August the men were using what remained and gathering limpets and seaweed along the shore

Shackleton secured a fourth opportunity The Chilean government provided Yelcho a small steam tug commanded by naval officer Luis Pardo It was not an icebreaker The ship could not force its way through a solid barrier of pack ice On August 25 Yelcho departed with Shackleton aboard As the pack

ice shifted toward the northeast Shackleton chose to approach Elephant Island from the northwest Pardo then had to bring the vessel safely through the waters near the island In fog he navigated among numerous grounded icebergs guiding the small tug toward the camp On August 30 Yelcho reached

Elephant Island The men ashore were preparing food when a cry announced the approaching ship At first the words Ship O were mistaken for Lunch O Then the men saw the vessel After more than four months of isolation a ship had reached their shore Pardo brought Yelcho

close enough for the evacuation to begin All twenty-two men who had remained on Elephant Island were taken aboard Every one of them was alive The wider Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition had a different outcome On the opposite side of Antarctica the separate Ross Sea Party suffered its own ordeal

and three men died The planned crossing of Antarctica was never completed But the twenty-two men rescued from Elephant Island together with the six who had sailed for help accounted for every member of the Endurance party The expedition lost its ship All twenty-eight men came home alive
